analysis.one_liner: Caps malpractice compensation for pain and suffering while adding patient-safety reporting and insurance rate rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: with zero cosponsors it was referred to two House committees, sent to a Health subcommittee, and died there when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would cap what a patient can recover for pain and suffering from a malpractice injury or death at $250,000 adjusted for inflation from 1975 (about $878,000 by 2005, per the bill's own estimate). It would also require courts to dismiss malpractice suits unless the filer certifies the claim has support, with escalating sanctions for violations. Offsetting the cap, it would create a national public database of physician discipline and patient complaints, fund mediation programs to resolve malpractice claims without lawsuits, protect patient-safety reports from being used in litigation, and require malpractice insurers to pass at least half of their cap-related savings to physicians through lower premiums.
analysis.who_benefits: Physicians and their malpractice insurers gain the most: the damage cap limits payouts, and insurers are required to pass at least half of the resulting savings to doctors as lower premiums. Hospitals and providers gain liability protection for good-faith reporting about colleagues to state medical boards, and a privilege keeps patient-safety work product out of lawsuits. Patients gain modestly from public disclosure of each physician's malpractice payments and disciplinary history and from being able to track complaints to state boards.

how_it_helps.text: Caps non-economic damages at $250,000 adjusted for inflation from 1975 — roughly $878,000 in 2005 by the bill's own estimate — which lowers malpractice insurers' payouts and, by extension, doctors' premiums.
Requires each malpractice insurer to develop a savings estimate and dedicate at least 50% of savings to reducing physician premiums, backed by civil penalties for noncompliance.

Requires public disclosure, by website or toll-free number, of each physician's education, specialty, malpractice payments, hospital discipline, criminal convictions, and state board discipline over the prior 10 years.
Creates an interstate database where patients can file and track complaints about physicians, with complaints kept confidential.
Authorizes grants to states and health care entities for voluntary mediation programs, modeled on Rush-Presbyterian-St. Luke's, to resolve malpractice allegations without litigation.
Protects health care providers from liability for good-faith reports to state medical boards about a physician's competence or conduct.
Extends sanctions, including contempt and fines, to attorneys who file malpractice claims without a certified factual basis.

analysis.who_pays: Patients catastrophically injured by malpractice pay the most: the cap applies to all providers in aggregate and limits recovery precisely for people whose losses are hardest to price in dollars — children, retirees, and patients who cannot work. Patient-safety records and mediation discussions become privileged and unavailable in lawsuits. Taxpayers fund the grant programs and the databases.
analysis.who_pays_short: Severely injured patients and malpractice plaintiff's lawyers

drawbacks.text: The $250,000 (inflation-adjusted) cap applies in the aggregate to all providers and covers only non-economic damages, so the people whose pain-and-suffering losses are largest — children, the elderly, and patients not in the workforce — bear the deepest cuts to compensation.
Patient safety work product is privileged: it cannot be subpoenaed, discovered, or admitted in civil or administrative proceedings, which keeps internal hospital analyses of errors out of lawsuits.

Every malpractice complaint must be dismissed unless the signer certifies factual and legal support, and violations bring mandatory contempt, costs, and escalating fines; such mechanisms can deter attorneys from taking valid but hard-to-document cases.

Insurers are required to pass only 50% of their savings from the cap to physicians in the form of lower premiums; the remainder stays with the insurers, and nothing in the bill directs savings to patients.
The bill's insurance 'reform' is a statement of intent that states should require hearings before malpractice-insurance rate increases; it does not directly mandate those rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency, complaint-tracking, and mediation provisions are real, patient-facing benefits that many states have since adopted in some form. But the bill's core is the damage cap, and its financial logic runs from injured patients to insurers and physicians: insurers pay out less, doctors' premiums fall, and the most seriously injured patients absorb the difference. The bill even routes the measurable savings to physician premiums rather than to patients. Weighing it honestly, the patient-safety gains do not offset a cap whose burden falls hardest on children, retirees, and others whose losses cannot be priced in lost wages.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with zero cosponsors, referred to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees, then sent to the Energy and Commerce Health subcommittee in September 2009, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Brian Baird, a Democrat, introduced the bill on July 31, 2009 — notably a member of the majority party sponsoring malpractice damage caps, an approach more often associated with Republicans.
No member of either party cosponsored the bill.
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced.
On September 8, 2009 it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, and no further action is recorded.
The bill never received a committee markup, hearing, or floor vote, and expired when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, injured patients kept the right to seek uncapped non-economic damages under state law, and plaintiff's lawyers kept the existing rules for filing malpractice suits. Physicians, malpractice insurers, and hospitals did not get the liability relief the bill would have given them; the patient-disclosure and complaint-tracking provisions never happened either.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so there was no recorded party split; the only measurable support was the sponsor himself, with zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The damage cap would substantially cut their payouts, and they would keep half the savings; against that, they would face state-level review of rate increases and mandates to certify premium reductions. Their gain from the cap comes directly out of compensation owed to injured patients.

Lower malpractice premiums, a cap on aggregate non-economic exposure, and immunity for good-faith reports to state medical boards. Lower premiums help patients only indirectly, and reduced liability weakens the financial deterrence on negligent care.

Mandatory dismissal for uncertified claims plus contempt and fines raise the cost and risk of taking malpractice cases, shrinking their business. Their interest here runs alongside their clients', since their fees come out of recoveries for injured patients.

Liability immunity for good-faith peer reporting and a privilege shielding patient-safety analyses from lawsuits reduce their litigation exposure. Those same privileges keep internal records of medical errors out of patients' suits.

The bill certifies patient safety organizations and gives their confidential work product legal privilege, locking in their role as the channel for error reporting — while making that information unavailable in litigation.
